weak_claims_to_re_research.claim: A mid-size SEA 3PL adding 20–50 carriers per month incurs $24,000–$216,000 annually in manual vetting labor costs
weak_claims_to_re_research.what_to_find: Find primary salary data for logistics operations coordinators in Singapore and Kuala Lumpur from a named-employer survey, government labor statistics (MOM Singapore, Malaysia DOSM), or a named HR consultancy report (Mercer, Korn Ferry) to validate the $25–$45/hour fully-loaded labor cost assumption. The annual cost range is the primary quantified SEA pain point in PP1.2 and its weakness undermines the entire SEA opportunity framing.

weak_claims_to_re_research.claim: Average cost of a successful fictitious pickup was $365,000 per incident in Q1 2024
weak_claims_to_re_research.what_to_find: Find an independent primary source for the per-incident cost of fictitious pickup or strategic cargo theft events beyond the single FreightWaves/Overhaul vendor citation. Candidates: TIA 2024 State of Fraud survey methodology (ask TIA for underlying data table); FBI IC3 2024 Internet Crime Report (check freight fraud subcategory); NICB cargo theft annual report; Verisk CargoNet breakdown by theft type. The $365K figure is cited in the top-line cost argument for PP1.1 but currently rests on a single vendor source.

weak_claims_to_re_research.claim: ASEAN road freight market is $119.43B in 2025 (used to anchor SEA opportunity TAM)
weak_claims_to_re_research.what_to_find: Find an independent cross-validation of the ASEAN road freight market size from a non-market-research-firm source. Candidates: ADB Transport Sector Assessment for ASEAN 2023–2024; ASEAN Secretariat ASEAN Transport Strategic Plan 2022–2026 with freight volume data; World Bank transport sector studies for Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia. The $119B figure from Mordor Intelligence is the only source and it anchors the entire SEA opportunity argument in both the value chain and PP1.2.

weak_claims_to_re_research.claim: Highway Q1 2026: 527,940 fraudulent emails blocked (+49.9% YoY); identity theft cases +89.6%; change-of-ownership fraud +169.6%; 50% of theft incidents tied to carriers with clean records
weak_claims_to_re_research.what_to_find: Find independent corroboration of Highway's Q1 2026 fraud trend statistics from a non-vendor source. Candidates: TIA April 2025 fraud report for comparable trend data; FBI IC3 2025 Annual Report (released mid-year); NICB 2024–2025 cargo theft data; CargoNet Q1 2026 quarterly release. The entire fraud-frequency argument in PP1.1 relies heavily on Highway self-reported data; if independent sources confirm similar trend magnitude, these claims can be upgraded to M.

weak_claims_to_re_research.claim: 26% of recorded cargo theft incidents in India, Indonesia, and Bangladesh involved insider participation
weak_claims_to_re_research.what_to_find: Access the actual BSI/TT Club 2024 Cargo Theft Report PDF to verify (a) whether the 26% figure applies to the three-country aggregate or to Indonesia specifically, (b) the sample size and methodology behind this calculation, and (c) whether Indonesia's insider-participation rate differs materially from the group average. If Indonesia-specific data is available, this would strengthen the SEA counterparty risk argument in PP1.2 and PP1.4 materially.

gate_reason: Stage 1 has a credible H-confidence backbone for the US market: Verisk CargoNet data, World Bank LPI, FMCSA government records, and multiple public-company M&A disclosures anchor the core problem-scale claims. However, 53% of total claims (41 of 77) score Low confidence. Three structural problems prevent a clean ship: (1) The primary SEA cost quantification — the $24K–$216K manual vetting labor estimate in PP1.2 — is explicitly tagged [ASSUMED-2] with no primary source, which means the SEA pain-point's economic argument is unsubstantiated. (2) Highway's fraud-frequency statistics (914,719 blocked attempts; +169.6% ownership fraud; 527,940 Q1 2026 blocks) constitute a large cluster of L-confidence vendor self-reports that drive the frequency narrative in PP1.1 and PP1.5 without independent corroboration. (3) The $119B ASEAN road freight figure from Mordor Intelligence is the only source for the market-size anchor of the SEA opportunity, and it is a secondary-market-research source with no multilateral or government cross-validation. The stage should ship for downstream use but must be flagged for deep-research on the three high-priority weak claims before the SEA opportunity framing and the US fraud frequency figures are cited as evidenced conclusions.

remediation_needed: PP count is 5 vs. target of 2–4; PP1.5 (beneficial-ownership cliff) is valuable but could be folded into PP1.1 RC5 to bring count within target range

PP1.2 root-cause RC3 cites only the stage's own value-chain map and its own ASSUMED notes as evidence — not an independent citation; remediation needed for this circular self-reference

Highway vendor statistics cluster (VC-10a, VC-18, VC-42, PP-1.1-freq-3, PP-1.1-rc2, PP-1.5-freq-1) forms a single-vendor data dependency across multiple pain points; independent corroboration required before promotion to final
